problem:
Let $V=C[0,3]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,3],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Given the functions $f(t)=t$ and $g(t)={e}^{t},$ which of the following statements are true?

- $⟨f(t),g(t)⟩=2{e}^{3}+1$
- $⟨f(t),g(t)⟩=1$
- $f(t)⊥g(t)$ with respect to the inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ in $V$
worked_solution:
First, we need to evaluate 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{3}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{t} & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =uv{|}_{0}^{3}-{\int }_{0}^{3}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}t \\  & =(t{e}^{t}){|}_{0}^{3}-{\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =(3{e}^{3}-0{e}^{0})-{e}^{t}{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =3{e}^{3}-({e}^{3}-1) \\  & =2{e}^{3}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now examine the statements:

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. This is as a result of the above calculations.

- Statement III is false. Since the inner product is not zero, our vectors are not orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
